verdict.rationale: The verb sphragizo (G4972) in Eph 1:13, Eph 4:30, and 2 Cor 1:22 attaches the seal of the Holy Spirit to those who believed, and in each case the agent is God or Christ and the believers are the sealed object. Its canon distribution fixes the sense: sealing a tomb for security (Matt 27:66), the Father sealing the Son to authenticate him (John 6:27), and sealing God's servants on the forehead to mark and protect them (Rev 7:3-8), so the act consistently means ownership, authentication, and security. The co-occurring arrabon (G0728), which is a hapax-rare term appearing only 3 times in the whole NT and always of the Spirit (Eph 1:14, 2 Cor 1:22, 2 Cor 5:5), is a commercial down-payment that guarantees the full sum, and Paul ties it to kleronomia (inheritance) and apolytrosis of God's peripoiesis (acquired possession). Eph 4:30 fixes the terminus with eis hemeran apolytroseos, the day of redemption. The Hebrew seal vocabulary (chatham, chotham, as in Hag 2:23, Jer 22:24, Song 8:6) supplies the same ownership and treasured-belonging background, so the pattern is pan-canonical. The one feature the words do not settle is whether the seal is unconditionally irreversible, since Eph 4:30 also carries a do-not-grieve warning, but they decisively affirm present sealing, ownership, and a guaranteed inheritance.

scripture.force: Aorist passive esphragisthete with an unstated divine agent, applied to those who heard the word of truth and believed, sealed by the promised Holy Spirit. The passive marks God as the actor and the believers as the sealed objects, with no other configuration of the verb anywhere in the corpus.

The Spirit himself is identified as arrabon tes kleronomias hemon, the down-payment of our inheritance, with the goal clause eis apolytrosin tes peripoieseos, the redemption of God's acquired possession. arrabon is a near-hapax (3 NT uses, all of the Spirit), a commercial earnest that legally guarantees the full sum, so the pledge plus inheritance plus possession plus redemption stack reads as a guarantee, not a bare token.

Aorist passive esphragisthete is reprised and given a forward terminus eis hemeran apolytroseos, fixing the seal's horizon to the day of redemption. The accompanying imperative me lypeite, do not grieve the Spirit, rests grammatically on the already-accomplished seal, which is the basis of the warning, not its prize.

God is the one bebaion, firmly establishing believers into Christ, and chrisas, anointing them. The participles set up the next verse where the same God seals and gives the Spirit as down-payment, so the four acts (establish, anoint, seal, give the earnest) share one divine subject.

Aorist middle sphragisamenos predicated of God, with the Spirit given as arrabona in believers' hearts. The combined sphragizo plus arrabon pattern matches Eph 1:13-14 exactly, establishing a consistent Pauline idiom in which the seal and the guarantee are the same indwelling Spirit.

Third and final NT occurrence of arrabon, again of the Spirit, with God as the one who prepared believers eis auto touto, for the future bodily redemption. This closes the down-payment idiom and confirms its eschatological force across two letters.

The Father sealed (esphragisen) the Son, where sealing means authenticating and marking as approved and owned. This calibrates the sense of the verb outside the Pauline sealing texts, showing seal carries ownership and authentication, not mere decoration.

The firm foundation has this seal (sphragis): the Lord knows those who are his. The noun explicitly glosses the seal as a mark of ownership and recognition, the same semantic that the verb carries in the anchor texts, which is why OpenBible links it strongly to Eph 1:13.

God will make his chosen one like a signet (chotham), a personal seal worn on the hand that marks treasured possession and delegated authority. This is the Hebrew background that grounds the seal-as-ownership imagery the NT vocabulary later carries, making the pattern pan-canonical rather than confined to one epistle.

complicating_texts.resolution: The imperative me lypeite, do not grieve the Spirit, could be read as making security conditional on behavior. But the relative clause en ho esphragisthete eis hemeran apolytroseos grounds the warning in an already-accomplished seal whose terminus is the day of redemption. Grammatically the seal is the basis of the exhortation, not a reward suspended on it, so the verse affirms present sealing while leaving the formal irreversibility question to inference rather than to the words themselves.

The aorist participle pisteusantes could be read as making the seal hinge on continuing faith. But it stands parallel to the aorist akousantes and both are antecedent, completed events relative to the sealing, not ongoing conditions, so the grammar locates faith as the occasion of the seal rather than a repeating condition of its continuance.

Circumcision is called a sphragis of the righteousness already held by faith, which shows the seal can be a confirming sign of a prior reality rather than the cause of it. This widens the attested sense of seal but does not weaken the Spirit-sealing texts, since in both cases the seal authenticates an existing standing before God.

variants.note: None of the anchor verses fall in the ingested ECM window (3 John 1.1 to 1.15), so they are not_in_ecm_scope. The minor articulation of the relative pronoun at Eph 1:14 does not touch the sealing or down-payment vocabulary, so no plausible variant changes the verdict.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads seal plus arrabon plus inheritance plus day of redemption as a single legal pledge structure. arrabon is a binding earnest that the giver cannot forfeit, the seal marks unalterable ownership, and the terminus is fixed at final redemption, so on its strongest form the vocabulary describes a guarantee that runs unbroken to the end. The proposition is affirmed in full.

Takes the me lypeite warning of Eph 4:30 and the confirming-sign use of sphragis in Rom 4:11 seriously, holding that the seal genuinely marks present ownership and pledges the inheritance, yet the words describe what God does for believers rather than formally foreclosing every possibility of apostasy. On its strongest form this lens still affirms that the Spirit seals believers and guarantees the inheritance, but treats the unconditional irreversibility of that guarantee as a question the seal and arrabon vocabulary state strongly but do not technically settle.

hermeneutics.notes: Both lenses affirm the proposition's core claim that the Spirit seals believers as God's possession and pledges their inheritance. They diverge only on whether the same vocabulary formally rules out forfeiture, which is a scope question the words leave to inference. Progressive revelation is true because the Hebrew signet and seal imagery is fulfilled and intensified in the NT Spirit-seal.

stem_audit.notes: The stem uses generic vocabulary that maps directly onto the Greek. seals corresponds to sphragizo, possession to peripoiesis, and guaranteeing inheritance to arrabon plus kleronomia, with no tradition-specific taxonomy loaded. The one word that leans toward a conclusion is guaranteeing, but it is a fair rendering of arrabon, which the lexical data confirms is a commercial guarantee, so the stem is not preloaded. The verdict is derived from the queried distribution, not from the stem.

lay_summary: Three of Paul's passages share one tight vocabulary pattern. In Ephesians 1:13 and 4:30 the verb sphragizo, to seal, appears as a passive with God as the unstated actor and believers as the object, and the seal is named as the promised Holy Spirit. Checking where this verb occurs across the canon settles its meaning: a sealed tomb for security, the Father sealing the Son to authenticate him, and God's servants sealed on the forehead to mark and protect them. So a seal means ownership, authentication, and security, never mere decoration. Ephesians 1:14 then calls that same Spirit the arrabon, a commercial down-payment that legally guarantees the full sum will follow. This word appears only three times in the whole New Testament, always of the Spirit, which makes its sense unusually focused. Paul links it to inheritance and to the redemption of God's acquired possession, and Ephesians 4:30 fixes the timeline by saying believers were sealed for the day of redemption. Second Corinthians 1 and 5 repeat the same stack: God establishes, anoints, seals, and gives the Spirit as the down-payment. The Hebrew background says the same thing, where a signet ring marks a treasured and authoritative possession. So the words run decisively in one direction: the Spirit marks believers as God's own and pledges their inheritance. There is one honest limit. Ephesians 4:30 also warns believers not to grieve the Spirit, and Romans 4:11 can call a seal a confirming sign of a standing already held. The seal and down-payment language strongly conveys lasting security, yet it does not by itself formally close the separate question of whether that security can ever be forfeited. That single scope gap, not any weakness in the core claim, is where careful readers diverge.
